title: New Creation
overview: How does the promise of renewal connect present discipleship with future hope?

sections.title: Reconciliation and a changed life
sections.text: Read Paul’s language of new creation within the surrounding account of Christ’s love and reconciliation. Notice how a changed way of seeing people connects with a calling to serve as ambassadors.

sections.title: Creation’s hope and God’s presence
sections.text: Romans describes creation groaning while waiting in hope. Revelation pictures God dwelling with his people and the end of death and mourning. Compare what is promised, what remains awaited and how believers live while waiting.

words.label: kainos · new
words.note: Compare its use in these passages without assuming the adjective alone settles how renewal takes place.

questions: How does reconciliation shape Paul’s description of new creation?
What is creation waiting for in Romans 8?
How might future hope shape care for people and the world today?

title: Living Letters
overview: Letters give sound a shape and words a form. Explore how the Sepher Yetzirah pictures the Hebrew alphabet as part of the formation of the world, and reflect on Scripture’s language of word, breath and life.

sections.title: A world formed through expression
sections.text:
In the Sepher Yetzirah, letters are more than marks on a page. They belong to a symbolic account of how the world takes shape through divine expression. Number, writing and sound offer different ways of approaching order and meaning: what can be counted, what can be formed into signs, and what can be spoken.

The title Book of Formation suits this emphasis. The work explores patterns of formation rather than retelling the sequence of Genesis. Here, “living letters” is our study title for that connection between language and life.

sections.title: Ten and twenty-two
sections.text:
The book begins with thirty-two paths of wisdom: ten sephiroth and twenty-two letters. In this account, the ten sephiroth belong to its treatment of number, spirit, elements and the directions of space. The twenty-two letters provide the alphabet through which forms and combinations are imagined.

The pattern holds variety within unity. Many letters and many forms belong to a creation whose source is one God. The numbers give the reader a framework for contemplation rather than a list of separate creators.

sections.title: Three families of letters
sections.text:
The twenty-two letters are arranged as three mothers, seven doubles and twelve simples. Each family connects language with patterns in the world, in time and in human life. The correspondences below follow the supplied Westcott edition.

Aleph, Mem and Shin receive particular attention. Aleph is associated with air, Mem with water and Shin with fire. Air mediates between the other two, pictured as a balance. The same pattern is carried into the seasons and the body: temperate conditions between heat and cold, and the chest between the head and belly.

letterGroups.name: Three mothers
letterGroups.connections: Air, water and fire; balance; temperate conditions, cold and heat; chest, belly and head.

entries.name: Aleph
entries.meaning: Air and mediation. Aleph stands between the water of Mem and the fire of Shin, giving the image of a balance that holds different forces together.
entries.usage: In the book’s correspondences, Aleph belongs to air in the world, temperate conditions in the year, and breath in the chest in the person. Read it with Mem and Shin to follow the same balancing pattern across all three settings.
entries.reflection: Where might listening and a measured response bring balance to opposing pressures?

entries.name: Mem
entries.meaning: Water. Mem belongs to the receptive side of the book’s elemental pattern, set alongside the fire of Shin with Aleph as mediator.
entries.usage: Mem is associated with water, with the earth in the world, with cold in the year, and with the belly in the person. Trace these as symbolic correspondences in chapter III rather than definitions of every Hebrew word containing Mem.
entries.reflection: What do the images of water and receptivity invite you to notice about receiving and sustaining life?

entries.name: Shin
entries.meaning: Fire. Shin brings the fiery side of the threefold pattern into view, set opposite Mem’s water and held in relation through Aleph’s air.
entries.usage: Shin is associated with fire, the heavens in the world, heat in the year, and the head in the person. Compare its place with Mem and Aleph to see how the book carries one pattern through world, year and person.
entries.reflection: How might the image of fire help you reflect on energy, intensity and the need for balance?

letterGroups.name: Seven doubles
letterGroups.letters: ב · ג · ד · כ · פ · ר · ת
letterGroups.names: Beth, Gimel, Daleth, Kaph, Peh, Resh, Tau
letterGroups.connections: Paired qualities such as life and death or peace and war; seven celestial bodies, days of the week and openings of perception.

entries.name: Beth
entries.meaning: Beth belongs to the seven doubles. This family expresses paired possibilities: life and death, peace and war, wisdom and folly, riches and poverty, grace and indignation, fertility and solitude, power and servitude. These are the family’s shared associations; no one pair is assigned to Beth here.
entries.usage: Read Beth within the sevenfold pattern of chapter IV: the seven celestial bodies, days of the week and openings of perception. The edition’s notes report differing assignments of individual letters to planets, so this study keeps those connections at the family level. As an illustration of the pairing described in chapter II, place Beth beside Aleph (בא) and reverse their order (אב). This illustrates how changing the order changes the arrangement; it does not assign a word meaning to the pair.
entries.reflection: Which contrast in this family draws your attention, and what choices does it invite you to consider?

letterGroups.name: Twelve simples
letterGroups.letters: ה · ו · ז · ח · ט · י · ל · נ · ס · ע · צ · ק
letterGroups.names: Heh, Vau, Zain, Cheth, Teth, Yod, Lamed, Nun, Samech, Oin, Tzaddi, Qoph
letterGroups.connections: Human activities and capacities; twelve zodiacal constellations, months and bodily organs.

entries.name: Heh
entries.meaning: Heh belongs to the twelve simples. This family connects letters with activities and capacities such as sight, hearing, speech, work, movement and sleep. These are shared associations of the twelve, rather than a fixed individual meaning assigned to Heh in this study.
entries.usage: Read Heh within the twelvefold pattern of chapter V: the zodiacal constellations, months of the year and bodily organs. The study follows the group-level relationships in the supplied English text without assigning one month, organ or activity exclusively to Heh. As an illustration of the pairing described in chapter II, place Heh beside Aleph (הא) and reverse their order (אה). This illustrates how changing the order changes the arrangement; it does not assign a word meaning to the pair.
entries.reflection: How might paying attention to a daily activity such as listening, working or resting change the way you live it?

sections.title: Letters in relationship
sections.text:
A single letter has possibilities that emerge when it meets another. The book describes the letters being paired and combined, giving the image of 231 gates. Pairing each of the twenty-two letters with every different letter, counting each pair once, gives 22 × 21 ÷ 2 = 231.

This pairing is different from rearranging all the letters in a group. Elsewhere, the book explores how changing an arrangement multiplies its possibilities. For this study, the central idea is relationship: the same small alphabet can take part in many expressions.

sections.title: World, year and person
sections.text:
The book repeatedly places its patterns in three settings: the universe, the year and the human being. Elements belong to the world; seasons and cycles belong to time; breath, perception and bodily life belong to the person. Its letter groups connect these settings through a shared symbolic order.

This invites a way of looking in which the person belongs within a larger whole. The correspondences express the source’s cosmology; they are not anatomical explanations or ordinary dictionary meanings of the letters.

sections.title: Reading alongside Scripture
sections.text:
Genesis 1 presents God speaking as creation takes form. Psalm 33 connects the heavens with God’s word and breath. Read these passages slowly, noticing who speaks, what happens and how creation responds. They offer a biblical starting point for reflecting on speech and life.

John 1 brings its own distinctive claim about the Word and the source of life. In 2 Corinthians 3, Paul describes people as a letter of Christ, written by the Spirit on human hearts. His image concerns a community shaped by God’s work. These passages can enter a conversation with the Book of Formation without assuming that Paul or John is teaching its alphabetic scheme.

sections.title: From contemplation to response
sections.text:
The source also calls for restraint in speech and attention to the heart. Its interest in letters is accompanied by the discipline of considering what can be spoken and how the mind is directed.

For personal reflection, ask how words give shape to relationships. What do our words communicate about the life within us? Paul’s image of a letter written on hearts offers a practical question to carry away: what might others read in the way we live?

words.label: dabar · word
words.note: Explore the Hebrew word used for “word” in Psalm 33:6, then compare the surrounding language of breath and command.

words.label: ruach · breath, wind, spirit
words.note: Compare the renderings in Genesis 1:2 and Psalm 33:6. Let each passage’s setting guide the reading.

words.label: gramma · letter
words.note: Read the contrast between letter and Spirit in 2 Corinthians 3:6 within Paul’s discussion of ministry and covenant.

questions: What changes when you think of a letter as sound and expression as well as a written shape?
How do the three families of letters connect the world, time and human life in this account?
Where do you see a shared interest in word and life between the source and the biblical readings? Where do their purposes differ?
What might it mean for your life to be a letter that others can read?

title: Sin
overview: How do Scripture’s accounts of wrongdoing lead towards confession and mercy?

sections.title: Wrongdoing and fractured relationships
sections.text: Observe the sequence of desire, action, hiding and blame in Genesis 3. Attend to what the story says about relationships with God and with one another before trying to build a definition from a single word.

sections.title: Confession and the need for grace
sections.text: Psalm 51 asks for mercy and renewal. Romans 3 places human accountability beside God’s action in Christ. Compare confession, cleansing and righteousness, taking care to follow the distinct argument of each passage.

words.label: chattat · sin
words.note: Check the context: the word can also be used in connection with a sin offering.

words.label: hamartia · sin
words.note: Study the word in sentences and arguments; an etymology alone cannot explain Paul’s account of sin.

questions: What forms of avoidance appear in Genesis 3?
What does the psalmist ask God to do?
How does Romans move from accountability to hope?

title: Redemption
overview: What does it mean to be rescued and brought into a new relationship with God?

sections.title: Rescue and belonging
sections.text: Read Exodus 6 in the setting of Israel’s forced labour. God’s promise includes both release from oppression and life as his people. Notice who acts, what is promised, and how the promise connects with the covenant.

sections.title: Redemption in Christ
sections.text: Ephesians places redemption within a larger account of blessing, forgiveness and hope in Christ. Read the whole paragraph before isolating a single image. Compare Peter’s language of ransom and ask how rescue changes the way believers live.

words.label: gaal · redeem
words.note: Trace the family and rescue settings in which this Hebrew verb occurs.

words.label: apolytrōsis · redemption
words.note: Compare its use in Ephesians 1:7 with the future hope in Romans 8:23.

questions: How do rescue and belonging connect in these passages?
What does each passage say redemption is from, and what is it for?
What response does Peter call for in the surrounding verses?

title: Sanctification
overview: What does belonging to God mean for daily life?

sections.title: Set apart for God
sections.text: Read Leviticus within its covenant setting. Notice the commands to the people alongside the statement about God making them holy. Consider how belonging and conduct are held together.

sections.title: A life shaped by that belonging
sections.text: Paul connects holiness with embodied choices and the treatment of other people. Compare the description of the Corinthians with the instructions that follow. Look for both what God has done and what the community is called to practise.

words.label: qadash · make holy
words.note: Explore how this verb is used of people, places and objects.

words.label: hagiasmos · sanctification
words.note: Compare translations and consider the specific conduct in 1 Thessalonians 4.

questions: Who acts in making a people holy?
Which ordinary choices receive attention in these readings?
What practice could help you respond to one of these commands?

title: Justification
overview: How do the biblical writers connect righteousness, faith and a life of obedience?

sections.title: Read Paul’s argument
sections.text: Romans 3 follows an extended account of human wrongdoing. Track the relationship between grace, faith and boasting, then follow the argument into Romans 4. Ask what Abraham’s story contributes to Paul’s explanation.

sections.title: Read James alongside Paul
sections.text: James examines a claim to faith that leaves a neighbour without practical help. Attend to the question each author addresses and the examples each uses. Christian traditions explain the relationship between justification and works differently; begin by describing each passage on its own terms.

words.label: dikaiōsis · justification
words.note: Compare Romans 4:25 and 5:18 within their surrounding arguments.

questions: What grounds for boasting does Paul exclude?
What kind of faith is James questioning?
How might these passages shape both assurance and care for others?
